claim: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is estimated to affect approximately 300 million individuals worldwide.
source: Major depressive disorder (MDD), also known as depression, is estimated to affect approximately 300 million individuals worldwide and is a leading cause of disability according to the World Health Organization (World Health Organization, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2017

claim: MDD is a leading cause of disability according to the World Health Organization.
source: Major depressive disorder (MDD), also known as depression, is estimated to affect approximately 300 million individuals worldwide and is a leading cause of disability according to the World Health Organization (World Health Organization, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2017

claim: Almost 30% of MDD patients fail to respond to one or more adequate antidepressants and thus exhibit treatment-resistant depression (TRD).
source: Almost 30% of MDD patients fail to respond to one or more adequate antidepressants and thus exhibit treatment-resistant depression (TRD; Conway et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Conway et al., 2017

claim: TRD is associated with increased morbidity and healthcare costs as well as reduced life quality and work productivity.
source: TRD is associated with increased morbidity and healthcare costs as well as reduced life quality and work productivity, all of which significantly contribute to the overall burden of MDD (Mrazek et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mrazek et al., 2014

claim: Various nonpharmacological interventions have been explored as therapeutic options for TRD, including repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), transcranial direct current stimulation, vagus nerve stimulation, epidural cortical stimulation, electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) and deep brain stimulation (DBS).
source: Because of the limited effectiveness of available psychological and pharmacological treatments for chronic TRD, various nonpharmacological interventions, including repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), transcranial direct current stimulation, vagus nerve stimulation, epidural cortical stimulation, electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) and deep brain stimulation (DBS), have been explored as therapeutic options for TRD (Wong and Licinio, 2001; Shelton et al., 2010; Cusin and Dougherty, 2012; Dandekar et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wong and Licinio, 2001; Shelton et al., 2010; Cusin and Dougherty, 2012; Dandekar et al., 2018

claim: Available treatment choices for TRD often have low response rates, multiple (often intolerable) side effects, and substantial lag times before a response is achieved.
source: However, these available treatment choices often have low response rates, multiple (often intolerable) side effects, and substantial lag times before a response is achieved.
evidence: Supported by general knowledge and context from the manuscript

claim: Rapid antidepressant effects are critical for patients with suicidal ideation, who account for 15% of TRD patients.
source: Lag time is especially dangerous and undesirable because rapid antidepressant effects are critical for patients with suicidal ideation, who account for 15% of TRD patients.
evidence: Stated as fact in the manuscript without specific citation

claim: DBS emerged in 2005 as a promising strategy for the management of TRD.
source: DBS emerged in 2005 and developed into a promising strategy for the management of TRD (Mayberg et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mayberg et al., 2005

claim: Clinical and preclinical studies have shown that DBS targeting various brain regions can induce remission of depressive symptoms.
source: Clinical and preclinical studies have shown that DBS targeting various brain regions, including the subcallosal cingulate, the ventral capsule/ventral striatum, medial forebrain bundle, nucleus accumbens (NAc), and lateral habenular nucleus (LHb), can induce remission of depressive symptoms (Anderson et al., 2012; Dandekar et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Anderson et al., 2012; Dandekar et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2018

claim: The response rates and effectiveness of DBS have varied widely among studies.
source: However, the response rates and effectiveness have varied widely among studies.
evidence: Stated as observation from literature review

claim: Most studies on DBS for TRD have focused on the long-term effects, on the order of days to weeks.
source: In addition, most studies have focused on the long-term effects of DBS, on the order of days to weeks; few have investigated the short-term, rapid antidepressant effects (Wang et al., 2020; Scangos et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2020; Scangos et al., 2021

claim: The mechanisms underlying the therapeutic response to DBS remain unclear.
source: The mechanisms underlying the therapeutic response to DBS remain unclear.
evidence: Stated as current state of knowledge

claim: The LHb innervates multiple brain regions and directly influences the serotonergic, noradrenergic, and dopaminergic brain systems.
source: Accumulating evidence indicates that the LHb, which innervates multiple brain regions and directly influences the serotonergic, noradrenergic, and dopaminergic brain systems, exhibits hyperactivity in depressed states (Hikosaka, 2010; Hu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hikosaka, 2010; Hu et al., 2020

claim: The LHb exhibits hyperactivity in depressed states.
source: Accumulating evidence indicates that the LHb, which innervates multiple brain regions and directly influences the serotonergic, noradrenergic, and dopaminergic brain systems, exhibits hyperactivity in depressed states (Hikosaka, 2010; Hu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hikosaka, 2010; Hu et al., 2020

claim: Electrical stimulation of the LHb improved depressive-like behavior in rat models of TRD.
source: Electrical stimulation of the LHb improved depressive-like behavior in rat models of TRD (Meng et al., 2011; Lim et al., 2015; Tchenio et al., 2017; Jakobs et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Meng et al., 2011; Lim et al., 2015; Tchenio et al., 2017; Jakobs et al., 2019

claim: A recent case report observed both short- and long-term improvements in depression, anxiety, and sleep in one human patient after administering high-frequency DBS to the left LHb.
source: A recent case report observed both short- and long-term improvements in depression, anxiety, and sleep in one human patient after administering high-frequency DBS to the left LHb (Wang et al., 2020), suggesting that LHb-DBS may represent a potential form of rapid-acting antidepressant therapy.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2020

claim: LHb-DBS may represent a potential form of rapid-acting antidepressant therapy.
source: A recent case report observed both short- and long-term improvements in depression, anxiety, and sleep in one human patient after administering high-frequency DBS to the left LHb (Wang et al., 2020), suggesting that LHb-DBS may represent a potential form of rapid-acting antidepressant therapy.
evidence: Inference based on case report cited (Wang et al., 2020)

claim: The efficacy of rapid-acting antidepressant therapy with LHb-DBS and its underlying mechanism remains elusive due to small sample sizes and open label design of relevant studies.
source: However, due to the small sample sizes and open label design of relevant studies, the efficacy of this rapid-acting antidepressant therapy and its underlying mechanism remains elusive.
evidence: Stated as limitation of existing literature

claim: LHb-DBS induced an immediate (within seconds to minutes) alleviation of depressive-like symptoms with a high-response rate in WKY and LPS-treated rats.
source: In this study, we observed an immediate (within seconds to minutes) alleviation of depressive-like symptoms with a high-response rate under DBS targeting the LHb (LHb-DBS) in two rat models of depression, Wistar Kyoto (WKY) and lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-treated rats.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: The remission of depressive symptoms under LHb-DBS manifested as a significantly increased sucrose preference, decreased immobility time in the forced-swim test, and increased locomotor activity.
source: The remission of depressive symptoms manifested as a significantly increased sucrose preference, decreased immobility time in the forced-swim test, and increased locomotor activity, including increased activity in the center area of an open arena.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: LHb-DBS activated multiple regions in afferent and efferent circuitry of the LHb, including those in limbic, serotonergic and dopaminergic systems.
source: LHb-DBS activated multiple regions in afferent and efferent circuitry of the LHb, including those in limbic, serotonergic and dopaminergic systems.
evidence: Supported by fMRI data presented in the manuscript

claim: The activation levels of brain regions connected to the medial LHb (M-LHb) were correlated with the extent of behavioral improvements.
source: The activation levels of brain regions connected to the medial LHb (M-LHb) was correlated with the extent of behavioral improvements.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of fMRI and behavioral data

claim: Rats with more medial stimulation sites in the LHb exhibited greater antidepressant effects than those with more lateral stimulation sites.
source: Rats with DBS sites more medial in the LHb exhibited greater antidepressant effects than those with more lateral DBS sites.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing different stimulation locations

claim: The antidromic activation of the limbic system and orthodromic activation of the monoaminergic systems connected to the M-LHb played a critical role in the rapid antidepressant effects of LHb-DBS.
source: These results indicated that the antidromic activation of the limbic system and orthodromic activation of the monoaminergic systems connected to the M-LHb played a critical role in the rapid antidepressant effects of LHb-DBS.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data and correlation analyses

claim: M-LHb-DBS might act as a valuable, rapid-acting antidepressant therapeutic strategy for treatment-resistant depression.
source: This study indicates that M-LHb-DBS might act as a valuable, rapid-acting antidepressant therapeutic strategy for treatment-resistant depression and demonstrates the potential of using fMRI activation of specific brain regions as biomarkers to predict and evaluate antidepressant efficacy.
evidence: Inference based on experimental findings

claim: fMRI activation of specific brain regions may serve as biomarkers to predict and evaluate antidepressant efficacy.
source: This study indicates that M-LHb-DBS might act as a valuable, rapid-acting antidepressant therapeutic strategy for treatment-resistant depression and demonstrates the potential of using fMRI activation of specific brain regions as biomarkers to predict and evaluate antidepressant efficacy.
evidence: Inference based on correlation between fMRI activation and behavioral outcomes

claim: The WKY rat is characterized as an animal model of endogenous depression.
source: The WKY rat is characterized as an animal model of endogenous depression and exhibits a set of behavioral abnormalities that emulate many symptoms observed in depressive patients, such as increased emotionality and reactivity to stress as well as considerable resistance to classic antidepressants (Will et al., 2003; Aleksandrova et al., 2019; Planchez et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Will et al., 2003; Aleksandrova et al., 2019; Planchez et al., 2019

claim: WKY rats exhibit behavioral abnormalities that emulate many symptoms observed in depressive patients, such as increased emotionality and reactivity to stress as well as considerable resistance to classic antidepressants.
source: The WKY rat is characterized as an animal model of endogenous depression and exhibits a set of behavioral abnormalities that emulate many symptoms observed in depressive patients, such as increased emotionality and reactivity to stress as well as considerable resistance to classic antidepressants (Will et al., 2003; Aleksandrova et al., 2019; Planchez et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Will et al., 2003; Aleksandrova et al., 2019; Planchez et al., 2019

claim: Depressive WKY rats exhibited a significantly lower sucrose preference compared to normal SD rats (0.49±0.01 versus 0.84±0.02).
source: As shown in Figure 2a, compared to normal Sprague‒Dawley (SD, Control) rats, depressive WKY rats exhibited a significantly lower sucrose preference in the sucrose preference test (SPT, 0.49±0.01 versus 0.84±0.02, mean ± SEM, n=10, same for below)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a

claim: Depressive WKY rats spent more time immobile in the forced swim test compared to normal SD rats (193±17 s versus 88±14 s).
source: As shown in Figure 2a, compared to normal Sprague‒Dawley (SD, Control) rats, depressive WKY rats exhibited a significantly lower sucrose preference in the sucrose preference test (SPT, 0.49±0.01 versus 0.84±0.02, mean ± SEM, n=10, same for below) and spent more time immobile in the forced swim test (FST, 193±17 s versus 88±14 s).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a

claim: Lower sucrose preference indicates anhedonia.
source: Lower sucrose preference and longer durations of immobility in the FST indicate anhedonia and despair-like behavior, respectively.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in behavioral neuroscience

claim: Longer durations of immobility in the FST indicate despair-like behavior.
source: Lower sucrose preference and longer durations of immobility in the FST indicate anhedonia and despair-like behavior, respectively.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in behavioral neuroscience

claim: WKY rats exhibited decreased locomotor activity in the OFT, including significantly reduced average speed and increased durations of immobility.

claim: WKY rats exhibited almost no entries into the center of the open field and spent no time in that area.
source: In addition, these WKY rats exhibited almost no entries into the center of the open field and spent no time in that area (Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a

claim: An intraperitoneal injection of LPS increases the levels of inflammatory factors, resulting in depression-like behavior.
source: An intraperitoneal injection of LPS is known to increase the levels of inflammatory factors, resulting in depression-like behavior (Cui et al., 2018; Planchez et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2020a).

claim: LPS-treated Wistar rats exhibited a significant reduction in sucrose preference and locomotor activity.

evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b

claim: The numbers of entries, time spent within, and total distance traveled in the center area of the OFT were significantly reduced in LPS-treated rats.
source: The numbers of entries, time spent within, and total distance traveled in the center area of the OFT were also significantly reduced (Figure 2b, n=9 rats).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b

claim: No significant change was observed in the immobility time in the FST for LPS-treated rats.
source: No significant change was observed in the immobility time in the FST (Figure 2b, n=9 rats).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b

claim: LPS administration at lower doses did not alter behavioral performance in the FST.
source: This finding is consistent with previous observations that LPS administration at lower doses did not alter behavioral performance in the FST (Tonelli et al., 2008; Pitychoutis et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tonelli et al., 2008; Pitychoutis et al., 2009

claim: High-frequency stimulation consisting of 130 Hz constant-current pulses with an amplitude of 300 μA and a duration of 90 μs was applied to the GF bipolar microelectrodes implanted in rat models of depression.
source: High-frequency stimulation consisting of 130 Hz constant-current pulses with an amplitude of 300 μA and a duration of 90 μs (biphasic and symmetric) was applied to the GF bipolar microelectrodes implanted in rat models of depression.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: After 15 min of LHb-DBS, the sucrose preference index (SPI) of the WKY rats increased from 0.49±0.01 to 0.84±0.04.

claim: Rats with more medial DBS sites had stronger BOLD activation in septum, DBN, LPO, LHA, IPN/VTA, DRN, and SLEA than rats with more lateral DBS sites.

claim: ECT produced a prompt improvement in symptoms of depression in the majority of patients treated.

claim: The relatively higher risk of side effects, such as cognitive impairment, limits the application of ECT treatment.
source: However, the relatively higher risk of side effects, such as cognitive impairment, limits the application of this treatment.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about ECT

claim: Ketamine administration showed a rapid effect (within hours) in patients with TRD, and this effect lasted up to 1–2 weeks.
source: Ketamine administration also showed a rapid effect (within hours) in patients with TRD, and this effect lasted up to 1–2 weeks.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about ketamine

claim: There are issues surrounding the long-term efficacy and safety of repeated administration of ketamine.
source: However, there are issues surrounding the long-term efficacy and safety of repeated administration of ketamine (Corriger and Pickering, 2019; Krystal et al., 2019).

claim: Out of the 19 WKY and LPS-treated rats, 16 (~84.2%) exhibited a sucrose preference increase greater than 50%.
source: In our studies, we found that out of the 19 WKY and LPS-treated rats, 16 (~84.2%) exhibited a sucrose preference increase greater than 50%, 13 (~68.4%) showed an increase in average speed greater than fivefold, and 14 (~73.7%) had at least one entry into the center area in the OFT.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The WKY and LPS-treated depressive rat models share similar characteristics, including abnormalities in various neurotransmitter and endocrine systems and emotional changes resulting from inflammatory stimuli.
source: The WKY and LPS-treated depressive rat models share similar characteristics, including abnormalities in various neurotransmitter and endocrine systems and emotional changes resulting from inflammatory stimuli.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about these animal models

claim: Classic antidepressants used in humans, such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, cause an antidepressant reaction in WKY rats.
source: Previous research indicates that classic antidepressants used in humans, such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, also cause an antidepressant reaction in WKY rats.
evidence: Based on previous research

claim: Ketamine has been shown to be effective in both WKY and LPS-treated rats.
source: Ketamine, a rapid-acting antidepressant in clinical practice, has been shown to be effective in both WKY and LPS-treated rats (Aleksandrova et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2020a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aleksandrova et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2020a

claim: DBS of the NAc increased exploratory activity and exerted anxiolytic effects in WKY rats.
source: In WKY rats, DBS of the NAc increased exploratory activity and exerted anxiolytic effects, and NAc-DBS was found to be effective for TRD treatment in humans (Dandekar et al., 2018; Aleksandrova et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dandekar et al., 2018; Aleksandrova et al., 2019

claim: NAc-DBS was found to be effective for TRD treatment in humans.
source: In WKY rats, DBS of the NAc increased exploratory activity and exerted anxiolytic effects, and NAc-DBS was found to be effective for TRD treatment in humans (Dandekar et al., 2018; Aleksandrova et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dandekar et al., 2018; Aleksandrova et al., 2019

claim: No animal model of depression can completely replicate human symptoms.
source: However, no animal model of depression can completely replicate human symptoms, and further research is necessary to validate our findings in human patients.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about animal models

claim: The LHb receives afferent inputs mainly from the limbic forebrain regions and the basal ganglia, which funnel through largely parallel circuits to reach the M-LHb and L-LHb, respectively.
source: The LHb receives afferent inputs mainly from the limbic forebrain regions and the basal ganglia, which funnel through largely parallel circuits to reach the M-LHb and L-LHb, respectively (Hu et al., 2020).

claim: No obvious activation was observed in basal ganglia regions afferent to the L-LHb.
source: No obvious activation was observed in basal ganglia regions afferent to the L-LHb.

claim: Except for the mPFC, all the activated afferent regions were in the limbic areas connected to the M-LHb.
source: Except for the mPFC, which is an afferent connection of the L-LHb, all the activated afferent regions were in the limbic areas connected to the M-LHb.

claim: The activation levels of limbic areas showed a strong correlation with the extent of the alleviation of depressive symptoms.
source: The activation levels of these limbic areas showed a strong correlation with the extent of the alleviation of depressive symptoms.

claim: The correlation between mPFC activation and behavioral improvement was not observed.
source: However, this correlation was not observed in the mPFC.

claim: The VTA and DRN are regions efferent from the LHb activated by LHb-DBS and are connected to the M-LHb.
source: The VTA and DRN are regions efferent from the LHb activated by LHb-DBS; these regions are also connected to the M-LHb.
evidence: Supported by fMRI data and anatomical knowledge

claim: The activation levels of the VTA and DRN were correlated with the antidepressant efficacy.
source: The activation levels of these two regions, especially that of the DRN, were also correlated with the antidepressant efficacy.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis

claim: The rostromedial tegmental nucleus, which receives the majority of LHb output and is efferently connected to the L-LHb, was not activated.
source: The rostromedial tegmental nucleus, which receives the majority of LHb output and is efferently connected to the L-LHb, was not activated.
evidence: Supported by fMRI data

claim: The immediate antidepressant effect of DBS mainly originated from the stimulation of the M-LHb and the antidromic and orthodromic activation of the circuits connected to the M-LHb.
source: All these results indicate that the immediate antidepressant effect of DBS mainly originated from the stimulation of the M-LHb and the antidromic and orthodromic activation of the circuits connected to the M-LHb, including the limbic, serotonergic and dopaminergic systems.

claim: Stimulation in more medial regions of the LHb produced more potent antidepressant effects than stimulation in more lateral regions.
source: This theory is further supported by the findings that stimulation in more medial regions of the LHb produced more potent antidepressant effects than stimulation in more lateral regions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Bursts of neuronal firing, an electrophysiological characteristic related to depression, occurred preferentially in the M-LHb instead of the L-LHb.
source: In addition, previous studies found that bursts of neuronal firing, an electrophysiological characteristic related to depression, occurred preferentially in the M-LHb instead of the L-LHb (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2018

claim: The SLEA is a region with multiple connections to other limbic brain regions and potentially capable of coordinating activity in different areas of the limbic lobe forebrain involved in emotional processing.
source: The SLEA is a region with multiple connections to other limbic brain regions and potentially capable of coordinating activity in different areas of the limbic lobe forebrain involved in emotional processing (Abler et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Abler et al., 2007

claim: The activation of the SLEA by LHb-DBS was mediated by the activation of limbic brain structures.
source: We suspect that the activation of the SLEA by LHb-DBS was mediated by the activation of limbic brain structures.

claim: The Cg and RS have resting-state functional connections with the habenula in humans.

evidence: Supported by citations to Ely et al., 2016; Torrisi et al., 2017

claim: The functional connection between Cg/RS and habenula was associated with subclinical depression scores.
source: This connection was associated with subclinical depression scores (Ely et al., 2016).

claim: The Cg has been investigated as a potential predictive biomarker of treatment response in depression across diverse treatment modalities.
source: Although the Cg has been investigated as a potential predictive biomarker of treatment response in depression across diverse treatment modalities, including antidepressant medications, evidence-based psychotherapy, rTMS, and ECT (Ge et al., 2020), we did not observe any correlation of Cg activation level with antidepressant efficacy in the present study.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ge et al., 2020

claim: No correlation of Cg activation level with antidepressant efficacy was observed in the present study.
source: Although the Cg has been investigated as a potential predictive biomarker of treatment response in depression across diverse treatment modalities, including antidepressant medications, evidence-based psychotherapy, rTMS, and ECT (Ge et al., 2020), we did not observe any correlation of Cg activation level with antidepressant efficacy in the present study.

claim: The activation of the LHb-Cg/RS pathway did not play a critical role in the immediate antidepressant effect.
source: This suggests that the activation of the LHb-Cg/RS pathway did not play a critical role in the immediate antidepressant effect observed here.

claim: Both WKY and LPS-treated rats showed significant improvement in locomotor activity upon administration of LHb-DBS.
source: Upon administration of LHb-DBS, both WKY and LPS-treated rats showed significant improvement in locomotor activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: No obvious activation by LHb-DBS was observed in the motor cortex for either WKY or LPS-treated rats.
source: However, no obvious activation by LHb-DBS was observed in the motor cortex for either type of rat.
evidence: Supported by fMRI data

claim: The suppression of motor action in depressive rats arises from the inhibition of dopaminergic and serotonergic neurons in the VTA, substantia nigra pars compacta and raphe nuclei due to hyperactivity of the LHb.
source: It was reported that the suppression of motor action in depressive rats arises from the inhibition of dopaminergic and serotonergic neurons in the VTA, substantia nigra pars compacta and raphe nuclei due to hyperactivity of the LHb (Hikosaka, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hikosaka, 2010

claim: The improvement of the locomotor activity might have resulted from the reversal of motor suppression by activating the limbic and monoaminergic systems, such as the DRN and VTA.
source: The absence of motor cortex activation by LHb-DBS suggests that the improvement of the locomotor activity was not due to the direct activation of the motor circuit. Instead, this improvement might have resulted from the reversal of motor suppression by activating the limbic and monoaminergic systems, such as the DRN and VTA.
evidence: Inference based on experimental observations and literature

claim: Hyperactivity of the LHb plays a critical role in depression etiology.
source: Mounting evidence from animal and human studies indicates that hyperactivity of the LHb plays a critical role in depression etiology (Hikosaka, 2010; Hu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hikosaka, 2010; Hu et al., 2020

claim: DBS targeting the LHb might result in an immediate suppression of hyperactivity and modulate the transmission of monoamine neurotransmitters.
source: DBS targeting the LHb might result in an immediate suppression of hyperactivity and modulate the transmission of monoamine neurotransmitters, such as dopamine and serotonin, in interconnected brain areas, thus resulting in the immediate remission of depressive symptoms, including anhedonia, despair, and anxiety.
evidence: Speculation based on experimental findings and literature

claim: The DRN, as the main source of serotonin in the brain, exhibited the strongest correlation in activation level with behavioral improvement among all the brain regions.
source: Notably, the DRN, as the main source of serotonin in the brain, exhibited the strongest correlation in activation level with behavioral improvement among all the brain regions.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis

claim: The M-LHb sends direct glutamatergic projections to both serotonergic neurons and GABAergic neurons in the DRN.
source: The M-LHb sends direct glutamatergic projections to both serotonergic neurons and GABAergic neurons in the DRN, which in turn exert feedforward inhibition of serotonergic neurons in the raphe nucleus (Hu et al., 2020).

claim: GABAergic neurons in the DRN exert feedforward inhibition of serotonergic neurons in the raphe nucleus.
source: The M-LHb sends direct glutamatergic projections to both serotonergic neurons and GABAergic neurons in the DRN, which in turn exert feedforward inhibition of serotonergic neurons in the raphe nucleus (Hu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hu et al., 2020

claim: The reversal of the inhibition of DRN serotonergic neurons might play a critical role in the rapid antidepressant effect of LHb-DBS.
source: The strong correlation between the activation level and behavioral improvement in the DRN suggests that the reversal of the inhibition of DRN serotonergic neurons might play a critical role in the rapid antidepressant effect of LHb-DBS.
evidence: Inference based on correlation data and anatomical knowledge

claim: Previous DBS-fMRI studies of other brain targets for depression have failed to demonstrate reliable BOLD responses within the DBS target and brain areas near the electrode tracks due to severe artifact produced by conventional stimulating electrodes.
source: Previous DBS-fMRI studies of other brain targets for depression, such as the NAc, have failed to demonstrate reliable BOLD responses within the DBS target and brain areas near the electrode tracks due to the severe artifact produced by conventional stimulating electrodes (Knight et al., 2013; Albaugh et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Knight et al., 2013; Albaugh et al., 2016

claim: The small-to-absent artifact produced by the GF electrodes enabled full and unbiased mapping of fMRI activation patterns in all brain regions.
source: In addition to allowing in vivo localization of DBS sites within the LHb, the small-to-absent artifact produced by the GF electrodes used here enabled full and unbiased mapping of fMRI activation patterns in all brain regions, which is important for understanding the therapeutic mechanisms underlying DBS.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: Conducting fMRI studies on the same sets of animals used for behavioral tests is critical for revealing the neuromodulatory effects and underlying mechanism of DBS.
